raw_evidence.label: The Pudding essay — origin of the dataset
raw_evidence.content: This dataset was assembled by The Pudding — a digital publication for visual essays — for a February 2018 piece titled 'The Structure of Stand-Up Comedy' by Russell Goldenberg and Matt Daniels. The team took the Netflix caption (.srt) file of Ali Wong's 2016 special 'Baby Cobra' and manually annotated every line: when a new joke started and ended, whether it was nested inside a larger topic, how long the laugh was, and whether the line called back to an earlier bit. Four team members annotated the transcript independently, reviewed as a group, and merged their annotations into one dataset. Each row in ali-wong--captions.csv is one subtitle line; each row in ali-wong--topics.csv is one topic segment (nested up to six levels deep). The stated goal was to explain why one specific moment near the end of the routine got the biggest laugh of the night — and the answer turned out to be about structure, not punchlines.

raw_evidence.label: Ali Wong's Baby Cobra — the special itself
raw_evidence.content: Baby Cobra is a one-hour stand-up special filmed at the Neptune Theatre in Seattle in September 2015 and released on Netflix on Mother's Day 2016. Ali Wong — then a little-known writer on ABC's Fresh Off the Boat — was seven and a half months pregnant on stage, wearing a striped dress and red-framed glasses. She has said most of the tickets had to be given away because no one knew who she was. The special runs roughly 60 minutes and covers aging, marriage, and pregnancy; its material is bold, physical, and sexually explicit. Baby Cobra is widely credited as the breakthrough that turned Wong from a working writer into a household name, paving the way for her later specials Hard Knock Wife (2018), Don Wong (2022), and the Emmy-winning Netflix series Beef (2023).

raw_evidence.label: The laughter climax hypothesis
raw_evidence.content: The central claim of the Pudding essay is that Baby Cobra has a laughter climax — a single moment near the end (around the 50-minute mark) where audience laughter spikes — and that this spike happens because the punchline at that moment simultaneously closes three topics Wong set up earlier in the hour. In other words, the biggest laugh of the night is not a new joke at all; it is a structural payoff. This is an interpretive hook the analyst should test directly against the laugh column: where are the laughs loudest, and do they line up with the callback column in ali-wong--topics.csv?

Each row in ali-wong--captions.csv is one subtitle line; each row in ali-wong--topics.csv is one topic segment (nested up to six levels deep). raw_evidence.label: The Pudding essay — origin of the dataset
raw_evidence.content: This dataset was assembled by The Pudding — a digital publication for visual essays — for a February 2018 piece titled 'The Structure of Stand-Up Comedy' by Russell Goldenberg and Matt Daniels. The team took the Netflix caption (.srt) file of Ali Wong's 2016 special 'Baby Cobra' and manually annotated every line: when a new joke started and ended, whether it was nested inside a larger topic, how long the laugh was, and whether the line called back to an earlier bit. Four team members annotated the transcript independently, reviewed as a group, and merged their annotations into one dataset. Each row in ali-wong--captions.csv is one subtitle line; each row in ali-wong--topics.csv is one topic segment (nested up to six levels deep). The stated goal was to explain why one specific moment near the end of the routine got the biggest laugh of the night — and the answer turned out to be about structure, not punchlines.

raw_evidence.label: Ali Wong's Baby Cobra — the special itself
raw_evidence.content: Baby Cobra is a one-hour stand-up special filmed at the Neptune Theatre in Seattle in September 2015 and released on Netflix on Mother's Day 2016. Ali Wong — then a little-known writer on ABC's Fresh Off the Boat — was seven and a half months pregnant on stage, wearing a striped dress and red-framed glasses. She has said most of the tickets had to be given away because no one knew who she was. The special runs roughly 60 minutes and covers aging, marriage, and pregnancy; its material is bold, physical, and sexually explicit. Baby Cobra is widely credited as the breakthrough that turned Wong from a working writer into a household name, paving the way for her later specials Hard Knock Wife (2018), Don Wong (2022), and the Emmy-winning Netflix series Beef (2023).

raw_evidence.label: The three callbacks — gaps of 12, 33, and 46 minutes
raw_evidence.content: The entire hour contains exactly three explicit callbacks annotated by the Pudding team. All three land in the final nine minutes of the show, and each one reaches further back than the last: the 'hippies' callback at 49:43 reaches back to 16:35 (a 33-minute gap); the 'mom/third-world country' callback at 50:57 reaches all the way back to 4:46 (a 46-minute gap — nearly the entire show); the 'my pussy is wet again' callback at 56:48 reaches back to 44:24 (12 minutes). All three cluster in the pregnancy act, turning what looks like a free-standing third act into a retrieval engine that pulls forward from earlier threads.

raw_evidence.label: What each callback actually calls back to
raw_evidence.content: The three callbacks pull from three completely different branches of the show. 'Hippies' (49:43) returns to a bit at 16:35 where Wong described herself and her husband as 'big hippies' who 'do ayahuasca ceremonies' — the payoff is her fantasy-conception line 'please look me in the eye and remember to come with intention, OK?' 'Mom / third-world country' (50:57) returns to 4:46 in the getting-older macro-topic, where Wong explained her hoarding by saying her mom was from a third-world country — the payoff is her mother's response to a miscarriage: 'Uh, yeah. Where I'm from, that's like losing a pair of shoes.' 'My pussy's all wet again' (56:48) returns to 44:24, where she had whispered 'my pussy is not as wet as it used to be' — the payoff flips the complaint into 'soldier glue... Neosporin' mucus at 7.5 months pregnant. Each callback lifts a specific phrase out of an earlier bit and lands it as the setup for a new punchline.

raw_evidence.label: The Pudding essay — origin of the dataset
raw_evidence.content: This dataset was assembled by The Pudding — a digital publication for visual essays — for a February 2018 piece titled 'The Structure of Stand-Up Comedy' by Russell Goldenberg and Matt Daniels. The team took the Netflix caption (.srt) file of Ali Wong's 2016 special 'Baby Cobra' and manually annotated every line: when a new joke started and ended, whether it was nested inside a larger topic, how long the laugh was, and whether the line called back to an earlier bit. Four team members annotated the transcript independently, reviewed as a group, and merged their annotations into one dataset. Each row in ali-wong--captions.csv is one subtitle line; each row in ali-wong--topics.csv is one topic segment (nested up to six levels deep). The stated goal was to explain why one specific moment near the end of the routine got the biggest laugh of the night — and the answer turned out to be about structure, not punchlines.

raw_evidence.content: Baby Cobra is a one-hour stand-up special filmed at the Neptune Theatre in Seattle in September 2015 and released on Netflix on Mother's Day 2016. Ali Wong — then a little-known writer on ABC's Fresh Off the Boat — was seven and a half months pregnant on stage, wearing a striped dress and red-framed glasses. She has said most of the tickets had to be given away because no one knew who she was. The special runs roughly 60 minutes and covers aging, marriage, and pregnancy; its material is bold, physical, and sexually explicit. Baby Cobra is widely credited as the breakthrough that turned Wong from a working writer into a household name, paving the way for her later specials Hard Knock Wife (2018), Don Wong (2022), and the Emmy-winning Netflix series Beef (2023).

raw_evidence.label: The laughter climax hypothesis
raw_evidence.content: The central claim of the Pudding essay is that Baby Cobra has a laughter climax — a single moment near the end (around the 50-minute mark) where audience laughter spikes — and that this spike happens because the punchline at that moment simultaneously closes three topics Wong set up earlier in the hour. In other words, the biggest laugh of the night is not a new joke at all; it is a structural payoff. This is an interpretive hook the analyst should test directly against the laugh column: where are the laughs loudest, and do they line up with the callback column in ali-wong--topics.csv?

raw_evidence.label: The three callbacks — gaps of 12, 33, and 46 minutes
raw_evidence.content: The entire hour contains exactly three explicit callbacks annotated by the Pudding team. All three land in the final nine minutes of the show, and each one reaches further back than the last: the 'hippies' callback at 49:43 reaches back to 16:35 (a 33-minute gap); the 'mom/third-world country' callback at 50:57 reaches all the way back to 4:46 (a 46-minute gap — nearly the entire show); the 'my pussy is wet again' callback at 56:48 reaches back to 44:24 (12 minutes). All three cluster in the pregnancy act, turning what looks like a free-standing third act into a retrieval engine that pulls forward from earlier threads.

raw_evidence.label: What each callback actually calls back to
raw_evidence.content: The three callbacks pull from three completely different branches of the show. 'Hippies' (49:43) returns to a bit at 16:35 where Wong described herself and her husband as 'big hippies' who 'do ayahuasca ceremonies' — the payoff is her fantasy-conception line 'please look me in the eye and remember to come with intention, OK?' 'Mom / third-world country' (50:57) returns to 4:46 in the getting-older macro-topic, where Wong explained her hoarding by saying her mom was from a third-world country — the payoff is her mother's response to a miscarriage: 'Uh, yeah. Where I'm from, that's like losing a pair of shoes.' 'My pussy's all wet again' (56:48) returns to 44:24, where she had whispered 'my pussy is not as wet as it used to be' — the payoff flips the complaint into 'soldier glue... Neosporin' mucus at 7.5 months pregnant. Each callback lifts a specific phrase out of an earlier bit and lands it as the setup for a new punchline.

raw_evidence.label: Baby Cobra's three macro-topics: aging, marriage, pregnancy
raw_evidence.content: Although Wong touches many subjects — hoarding, HPV, sexual history, racial politics, feminism — the routine organizes them under three macro themes: aging, marriage, and pregnancy. The topics.csv file reflects exactly this hierarchy, with six levels of nesting: a top-level topic (level 1) like '6-getting older' contains level-2 sub-topics, which contain level-3 bits, and so on. A digression about HPV, for instance, is nested several levels deep inside a larger bit about sleep. This nesting is what makes callbacks possible: because a bit has a parent and siblings, you can return to it later from a completely different branch.

raw_evidence.label: The hour is basically two macro-topics: marriage and pregnancy
raw_evidence.content: Baby Cobra looks like it covers a dozen subjects, but the topic tree collapses into only six level-1 segments, and two of them — marriage and pregnancy — eat almost the entire hour. Marriage runs from 6:55 to 37:35 (1,840 seconds, 30.7 minutes), and pregnancy runs from 37:57 to 57:17 (1,160 seconds, 19.3 minutes). Together they account for 85% of the runtime. The other four level-1 segments — intro, getting-older, a 10-second paintball aside, and the conclusion — take up 9.5 minutes combined. In structural terms, the special is a two-act play with a cold open and a coda.

raw_evidence.label: Ali Wong's Baby Cobra — the special itself
raw_evidence.content: Baby Cobra is a one-hour stand-up special filmed at the Neptune Theatre in Seattle in September 2015 and released on Netflix on Mother's Day 2016. Ali Wong — then a little-known writer on ABC's Fresh Off the Boat — was seven and a half months pregnant on stage, wearing a striped dress and red-framed glasses. She has said most of the tickets had to be given away because no one knew who she was. The special runs roughly 60 minutes and covers aging, marriage, and pregnancy; its material is bold, physical, and sexually explicit. Baby Cobra is widely credited as the breakthrough that turned Wong from a working writer into a household name, paving the way for her later specials Hard Knock Wife (2018), Don Wong (2022), and the Emmy-winning Netflix series Beef (2023).

sentences.summary: det_04: Headline comedians target ~18s of laughter per minute. Source: Why Laughs Per Minute Is Not The Best Way To Judge Comedians (https://www.realfirststeps.com/13528/stand-up-comedy-laughs-per-minute/) Facts: Headline comedians target ~18+ seconds of laughter per performing minute; This is roughly 30% of stage time spent with audience laughing

raw_evidence.label: Headline comedians target ~18s of laughter per minute
raw_evidence.content: Industry guides on stand-up performance peg a headline-level comedian at roughly 18 or more seconds of audience laughter per minute on stage — i.e., the audience spends about 30% of the time laughing, not listening. That works out to 4–6 punchlines that actually get a laugh per minute. This gives us a concrete benchmark against which to measure Ali Wong: what share of the 60-minute special is laughter, how many laugh events there are, and whether individual topics sustain the 30% threshold or blow past it. It also tells us that raw 'jokes per minute' is the wrong metric — what matters is laughter time accumulated.

raw_evidence.content: Industry guides on stand-up performance peg a headline-level comedian at roughly 18 or more seconds of audience laughter per minute on stage — i.e., the audience spends about 30% of the time laughing, not listening. raw_evidence.label: Two laugh peaks, not one: 12:05 and 49:42
raw_evidence.content: Running a 60-second rolling window over the laugh track produces two near-identical peaks. The biggest peak is at t=725s (12:05) with 27.5 seconds of laughter in a single minute — the 'colonize the colonizer' bit inside the marriage act. The second peak is at t=2982s (49:42) with 27.2 seconds — the conception fantasy that closes the pregnancy act, right next to the '...come with intention' callback. The two peaks are statistically tied; the 49:42 climax that the Pudding essay built its story around is the STRUCTURAL peak even if it is not literally the single loudest second. Readers who expect Wong's funniest laugh to come from her funniest sentence are looking in the wrong place.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_08 ===")
runtime = int(cap["timeStop"].max()) + 1
laugh_per_sec = np.zeros(runtime)
for _, r in cap.iterrows():
    laugh_per_sec[int(r["timeStart"])] += r["laugh"]
rolling = np.convolve(laugh_per_sec, np.ones(60), mode="same")
top_idx = np.argsort(rolling)[::-1]
seen = set()
top_windows = []
for idx in top_idx:
    # Cluster peaks within 30s of an already-seen one
    if any(abs(idx - s) < 30 for s in seen):
        continue
    seen.add(int(idx))
    top_windows.append((int(idx), float(rolling[idx])))
    if len(top_windows) >= 5:
        break

print(f"Top 5 laughter peaks (60s rolling window):")
for t, val in top_windows:
    print(f"  t={t}s ({t//60}:{t%60:02d}) - {val:.1f}s laughter in 60s window")
print(f"Overall peak: t={top_windows[0][0]}s "
      f"({top_windows[0][0]//60}:{top_windows[0][0]%60:02d}) with "
      f"{top_windows[0][1]:.1f}s of laughter in a single minute")

raw_evidence.content: Ranked by total laugh-seconds per bit, the biggest wins are 'hooking up' (20.5s total, 35.1 laugh-s/min), 'bad drivers' (19.75s), '697-wet' (17.75s), and 'debt' (17.5s). raw_evidence.code:

    laugh_s=("laugh", "sum"),
    n_lines=("laugh", "size"),
    start=("timeStart", "min"),
    end=("timeStop", "max"),
).reset_index()
bits["dur_s"] = bits["end"] - bits["start"]
bits["laugh_per_min"] = bits["laugh_s"] / (bits["dur_s"] / 60)
bits = bits[bits["dur_s"] > 0]
top_bits = bits.nlargest(10, "laugh_s")
print("Bits with the most total laughter:")
print(top_bits[["group", "start", "dur_s", "n_lines",
                "laugh_s", "laugh_per_min"]].to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: What a callback is in stand-up
raw_evidence.content: A callback is a joke that refers to an earlier joke or premise from the same set. The laugh lands because the audience has to make the connection themselves: you told us about your hoarding 30 minutes ago, and now a reference to hoarding lands on top of a completely different bit. Comedians and teachers talk about callbacks as the move that turns a routine from a 'list of observations' into a 'cohesive narrative' — the audience gets an ah-ha moment and feels rewarded for paying attention. This is a central concept for the Pudding essay: it argues that Baby Cobra's biggest laughs are not stand-alone punchlines but callbacks that pull together plot threads set up much earlier, giving stand-up the satisfaction of a well-made screenplay.

This is an interpretive hook the analyst should test directly against the laugh column: where are the laughs loudest, and do they line up with the callback column in ali-wong--topics.csv?

raw_evidence.label: Callbacks out-laugh average minutes by 1.34x
raw_evidence.content: In the 30 seconds after each callback trigger, audience laughter totals 16.75s, 2.25s, and 6.0s — mean 8.33s. The baseline is a bootstrap of 1,000 random 30-second windows across the show: mean 6.23s. Callback moments out-laugh the baseline by about 1.34x. That effect is real but smaller than you would guess from a piece built around these three moments — because the callbacks' real payoff is that they chain INTO the conception bit at 50:11 ('That's right. 'Cause I don't wanna work anymore.'), which is the second-loudest line of the entire special. The callbacks do not land the biggest laugh directly; they set up the bit that does.

print("=== ana_10 ===")


def window_laugh(t0: int, length: int = 30) -> float:
    return float(cap[(cap["timeStart"] >= t0) &
                     (cap["timeStart"] < t0 + length)]["laugh"].sum())


cb_times = cb["timeStart"].tolist()
cb_laughs = [window_laugh(t) for t in cb_times]
print(f"Callback window 30s laugh totals: {cb_laughs}")
print(f"Mean callback-window laughter: {np.mean(cb_laughs):.2f}s")

np.random.seed(42)
runtime = int(cap["timeStop"].max())
baseline_starts = np.random.randint(0, runtime - 30, 1000)
baseline_laughs = [window_laugh(int(t)) for t in baseline_starts]
print(f"Baseline (1000 random 30s windows) mean: {np.mean(baseline_laughs):.2f}s")
print(f"Baseline median: {np.median(baseline_laughs):.2f}s")
print(f"Callback windows beat the baseline by "
      f"{np.mean(cb_laughs) / np.mean(baseline_laughs):.2f}x")

raw_evidence.label: Callbacks out-laugh average minutes by 1.34x
raw_evidence.content: In the 30 seconds after each callback trigger, audience laughter totals 16.75s, 2.25s, and 6.0s — mean 8.33s. The baseline is a bootstrap of 1,000 random 30-second windows across the show: mean 6.23s. Callback moments out-laugh the baseline by about 1.34x. raw_evidence.label: Ali Wong's Baby Cobra — the special itself
raw_evidence.content: Baby Cobra is a one-hour stand-up special filmed at the Neptune Theatre in Seattle in September 2015 and released on Netflix on Mother's Day 2016. Ali Wong — then a little-known writer on ABC's Fresh Off the Boat — was seven and a half months pregnant on stage, wearing a striped dress and red-framed glasses. She has said most of the tickets had to be given away because no one knew who she was. The special runs roughly 60 minutes and covers aging, marriage, and pregnancy; its material is bold, physical, and sexually explicit. Baby Cobra is widely credited as the breakthrough that turned Wong from a working writer into a household name, paving the way for her later specials Hard Knock Wife (2018), Don Wong (2022), and the Emmy-winning Netflix series Beef (2023).
